title: Mile's Home
description: You look toward the working corner of the apartment. The desk stands against the wall perpendicular to the window, with a shelf of books above it that makes the space feel close, personal, and lived in. It is cozy, but not tidy. There is the usual kind of programmer's clutter everywhere: cables coiled and tangled across the floor, Post-it notes and scraps of paper  with old reminders, crumpled printouts of BASIC and assembler code, five-inch floppy disks, and the small debris of long hours spent thinking at a machine. Across  the room, against the wall opposite the window, sits the sofa, set so you could watch the television or turn and look out at the city. The whole room feels warm, familiar, and comfortably disordered, like a place you genuinely likes to work in.
lore: Miles lives alone in a compact studio apartment inside a once-upscale early-1950s mixed-use building on the edge of San Vesper's old industrial district and downtown core. By 1987 the neighborhood has declined: office workers, aging tenants, cheap sublets, distant sirens, and neon reflecting off rain-stained concrete.

The apartment located on the 12th floor was originally converted from office space in the late 1970s. It is small but cozy, with high ceilings, wood-paneled walls, large windows facing the distant skyline, and old horizontal blinds filtering warm golden sunlight through layers of smog.
The studio is divided into a work area and a small kitchen near the entrance. Off-camera are a tiny sleeping nook and a compact bathroom. The space feels lived-in rather than stylish.
Miles spends much of his free time here reading, working, listening to tapes, or staring through the blinds toward the distant skyscrapers. He genuinely likes this place.

Legally, his living arrangement is questionable. The lease still belongs to an old friend who left the city years ago. Miles sublets unofficially under an old rent-controlled agreement dating back to the early 1980s housing crisis, which makes the apartment unusually affordable. He avoids drawing attention to himself.

The building has an underground parking garage where Miles keeps his worn 1972 Plymouth Satellite muscle car. By the late 80s cars like it are already outdated compared to newer Japanese imports, but it is still solid, loud, and powerful.
